Chapter 12: Distributed Transactions

12.1 Introduction

A distributed transaction is a transaction that spans multiple networked nodes. In a single-process database, atomicity and durability are enforced by a write-ahead log and a lock table; in a distributed system, we must additionally coordinate independent machines over an unreliable network, and we must do so in the presence of partial failure—the possibility that one machine crashes while the others continue running. Partial failure is the defining property of distributed systems, and it is what makes distributed transaction processing qualitatively harder than centralized transaction processing.

This chapter develops the machinery of distributed transactions from first principles. We will cover:

The failure model: crashes, message loss, network partitions, and the Two Generals problem.

Consensus and its impossibility: the FLP result and why it forces protocol designers to choose between liveness and safety.

Atomic commit: two-phase commit (2PC), its log protocol, its failure analysis, and three-phase commit (3PC).

Consensus-based commit: Paxos Commit and Raft-based commit, which use replicated state machines to make the coordinator itself fault-tolerant.

Isolation in distributed transactions: distributed deadlock detection, distributed two-phase locking, and snapshot isolation across nodes.

Practical concerns: write-ahead logging for distributed transactions, coordinator optimization, and the integration of these protocols into real systems.

Throughout, we will write working C code, since the details of logging, timeouts, and state transitions are exactly where distributed protocols go wrong in practice. The code is simplified but structurally faithful: the state machines, log records, and message flows correspond to those in production systems.

12.2 The Problem: Atomic Commit Across Machines

Consider a bank transfer from account A (stored on node N1) to account B (stored on node N2). The transfer is a transaction T with two participants:

T1 (on N1): debit A by $100.
T2 (on N2): credit B by $100.

The transaction is atomic only if both operations commit or both abort. If N1 commits the debit and N2 aborts the credit, $100 has vanished. If N1 aborts and N2 commits, $100 has been created. The database must prevent both outcomes, and it must do so even if N1 crashes mid-protocol, or the network between N1 and N2 goes down.

This is the atomic commitment problem:

Agreement: No two participants decide differently (one commits, another aborts).

Validity: If all participants vote COMMIT and no failure occurs, the transaction commits. If any participant votes ABORT, the transaction aborts.

Termination: All correct participants eventually decide.

Note the asymmetry: abort is one-way. A participant that aborts locally (e.g., because a local constraint failed) forces the whole transaction to abort, and this decision is irreversible once communicated. Commit, by contrast, requires unanimous agreement, and the commit decision must be durable at every participant before the transaction can be acknowledged.

The asymmetry arises because abort requires no coordination—a participant can abort unilaterally and discard its work—whereas commit requires every participant to have durably recorded its portion of the transaction, and this fact must be known to all participants before any of them can release locks and expose the results.

12.3 Failure Model

We adopt the standard crash-recovery model with the following assumptions:

Nodes: Each node has volatile memory (lost on crash) and stable storage (survives crashes, modeled as a log with atomic sector writes). Nodes crash and recover; a crashed node is eventually repaired and rejoins with its stable storage intact.

Network: Messages can be lost, delayed, duplicated, and reordered. The network is eventually reliable: if a node sends a message repeatedly to a non-faulty destination, the message is eventually delivered. This models TCP with retransmission, but we do not assume TCP itself; we will implement retransmission explicitly.

Clocks: We make no synchrony assumptions for the correctness of the protocols. Timeouts are used for liveness (to trigger retransmission and abort decisions), but correctness never depends on a timeout firing "at the right time."

Byzantine behavior: Nodes do not lie. A crashed node does not send contradictory messages. (Byzantine fault tolerance requires quorum-based protocols and is beyond this chapter.)

Crash-recovery subtlety: A node that crashes and recovers has lost its volatile state but retains its log. The log is the node's source of truth. Every protocol in this chapter is designed so that a recovering node can reconstruct its role and obligations from the log alone.

12.4 The Two Generals Problem

Before designing protocols, we must confront a fundamental limitation: two parties communicating over an unreliable network cannot achieve certainty about a shared decision.

12.4.1 The Problem Statement

Two generals, each commanding an army, occupy hills on opposite sides of a valley. They must coordinate an attack. If either attacks alone, the result is defeat; only a simultaneous attack succeeds. The generals can communicate only by messenger through the valley, and messengers may be captured (messages lost).

How can the generals agree on a time to attack?

12.4.2 The Impossibility

Suppose General A sends the message "Attack at dawn." A cannot know whether B received it. B, upon receiving it, sends an acknowledgment "Confirmed." B cannot know whether A received the confirmation. A, upon receiving the confirmation, sends "Confirmed the confirmation." And so on.

No finite sequence of messages suffices. The argument is by induction on the last message: consider the shortest protocol that solves the problem, and let M be its last message. The sender of M cannot distinguish between the case where M is delivered and the case where M is lost (since no message follows M in either case). But the outcome differs between these cases: if M is lost, the receiver does not know the decision, and the protocol cannot guarantee agreement. Hence no such protocol exists.

Formally: For any protocol P and any message history H that leads both generals to attack, there exists a history H' that is indistinguishable to the sender of the last message, in which the last message is lost, and in which the generals do not agree. Since the sender's behavior is identical in H and H', and the receiver's behavior differs, at least one general attacks without the other—violating the requirement.

12.4.3 Implications for Distributed Transactions

The Two Generals problem tells us that no protocol can guarantee atomic commit in a system with unreliable communication and no timeouts. If the coordinator sends COMMIT to a participant and the message is lost, the participant cannot distinguish "coordinator decided COMMIT but the message was lost" from "coordinator crashed before deciding." The participant must wait indefinitely or decide unilaterally (risking disagreement).

Every practical atomic commit protocol resolves this by introducing a timeout and accepting a weaker guarantee:

If a participant has not heard from the coordinator within a timeout, it can safely abort (in 2PC), because abort is always a safe unilateral decision for a participant that has not yet committed.

The cost is liveness: a transaction can be blocked if the coordinator crashes after sending COMMIT to some participants but before sending it to all. This is the blocking problem of 2PC, and we will analyze it in detail.

The key insight is that the timeout does not provide information—it provides a decision procedure in the absence of information. The participant's timeout-abort is correct not because the timeout tells the participant what happened, but because the protocol's invariant guarantees that unilateral abort is safe in the states where the participant finds itself.

12.5 Consensus and the FLP Impossibility Result

Atomic commitment is closely related to consensus: the problem of getting a set of nodes to agree on a single value. The FLP impossibility result (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985) shows that consensus cannot be solved deterministically in an asynchronous system with even a single crash failure.

12.5.1 The Model

FLP considers:

Asynchronous system: There is no bound on message delivery time or on processing time. A "slow" message is indistinguishable from a "lost" message.

Crash failures: Nodes may crash at any time. A crashed node sends no further messages.

Deterministic protocols: The protocol's next state is a deterministic function of its current state and the message received. (Randomized protocols are outside FLP's scope.)

Consensus: All non-faulty nodes eventually decide on a common value, and the value must be one proposed by some node (validity).

12.5.2 The Result

Theorem (FLP): In an asynchronous system with crash failures, no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee termination if even one node may crash.

The proof sketch is as follows (the full proof is in Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson, 1985):

Configurations and valence: A configuration is the complete state of the system (all node states plus all in-flight messages). A configuration is bivalent if there are executions from it leading to decision 0 and executions leading to decision 1. It is univalent if all executions from it lead to the same decision.

Initial bivalence: There exists an initial configuration (all nodes' initial states, no messages in flight) that is bivalent. This follows from a swapping argument: if we change one node's initial proposal from 0 to 1, and the decision changes, there must be a pair of adjacent configurations where the decision flips—and that pair is bivalent.

Inductive construction of a non-terminating execution: Starting from a bivalent configuration, we show that for any bivalent configuration C and any event e (delivery of a message to node p), there exists a bivalent configuration C' reachable from C without applying e. The argument: consider a chain of configurations from C applying e and then some other event e'. If applying e from C leads to a univalent configuration (say, 0-valent), then applying e' first and then e must lead to a different decision (1-valent), because e' is applicable to p in both cases and p cannot distinguish the order. But this contradicts the assumption that e from C is univalent. Hence e from C is bivalent, and we can defer e.

The construction: We build an infinite execution by always choosing a bivalent configuration and deferring some message delivery. The execution never decides, because a decision requires reaching a univalent configuration, and we always remain bivalent.

The critical step: The argument that "applying e from C leads to a univalent configuration" must be contradicted. The contradiction arises because node p is the same in both orderings, and p's state is the same after receiving the message in both orderings—so the decision must be the same. But the other events in between can change the decision. This is where the crash failure enters: we can crash node p (or defer p's messages) to make the two orderings indistinguishable to p.

12.5.3 Implications for Distributed Transactions

FLP tells us that atomic commit cannot be both:

Deterministic (no randomness),

Asynchronous (no timing assumptions),

Crash-tolerant (survives node crashes), and

Terminating (all correct nodes eventually decide).

Every real protocol gives up at least one of these properties:

2PC gives up termination: If the coordinator crashes at the wrong moment, participants block indefinitely. 2PC is correct (agreement, validity) but not terminating in the presence of coordinator failure.

3PC gives up asynchrony: 3PC assumes bounded message delay and uses timeouts to make progress. If the network is slow (messages delayed beyond the timeout), 3PC can violate agreement—two participants can decide differently.

Paxos Commit / Raft-based commit gives up determinism in the coordinator selection (leader election uses timeouts and can elect different leaders) but preserves agreement through quorum intersection. These protocols are terminating under partial synchrony (eventually the network stabilizes and a leader is elected).

Randomized protocols (e.g., Ben-Or's algorithm) give up determinism: they use coin flips to break symmetry, and termination is with probability 1.

The practical takeaway: In a real system, we must choose which guarantee to sacrifice. 2PC sacrifices liveness (blocking) for simplicity and correctness. Consensus-based commit sacrifices simplicity for liveness under partial synchrony. The choice depends on the system's availability requirements.

12.5.4 A Note on Randomization

FLP's impossibility applies to deterministic protocols. Randomized protocols can achieve consensus with probability 1 by using randomness to break symmetry. Ben-Or's algorithm (1983) is a classic example:

Each node proposes a value.

In each round, a node sends its current value to all others.

If a node receives a majority of identical values, it decides on that value.

Otherwise, it flips a coin and adopts the majority value (if any) or a random value.

Termination is guaranteed with probability 1: eventually, all nodes flip the same coin value in the same round, and the protocol converges. The expected number of rounds is O(2^n) for n nodes, which is impractical for large n but demonstrates the principle.

Modern randomized protocols (e.g., those using shared coins) achieve expected constant rounds. However, randomized commit protocols are rare in practice because the deterministic consensus protocols (Paxos, Raft) are well-understood and perform better under partial synchrony.

12.6 Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

Two-phase commit (Gray, 1978; Lampson and Sturgis, 1976) is the simplest correct atomic commit protocol. It is the workhorse of distributed databases and is used (in variants) by XA, Tuxedo, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and many others.

12.6.1 Roles

Coordinator: One node (typically the node that initiated the transaction) runs the commit protocol.

Participants: The nodes that executed parts of the transaction. Each participant has a vote.

12.6.2 Protocol Description

Phase 1 (Voting):

The coordinator sends a PREPARE (or VOTE-REQ) message to every participant.

Each participant processes the transaction to the point where it can either commit or abort unilaterally. It writes a "prepared" record to its log (forcing the log to stable storage) and then votes:

YES: "I am prepared to commit. My portion of the transaction is durable and undoable/redoable."

NO: "I have aborted locally (e.g., a constraint failed)."

If a participant votes YES, it enters the "prepared" state. In this state, it cannot unilaterally abort (its work is durable and it has promised to be able to commit) and it cannot unilaterally commit (it has not yet received the global decision). It must wait for the coordinator's decision.

If a participant votes NO, it aborts locally, releases locks, and forgets the transaction. It does not need to wait for the coordinator.

Phase 2 (Decision):

The coordinator collects votes. If all votes are YES, it decides COMMIT. If any vote is NO (or a participant fails to respond before a timeout), it decides ABORT.

The coordinator writes the decision to its log (forcing it to stable storage) and then sends COMMIT or ABORT to every participant.

Each participant, upon receiving the decision, writes a "commit" or "abort" record to its log, releases locks, and acknowledges (ACK) to the coordinator.

The coordinator, upon receiving ACKs from all participants, writes an "end" record to its log and forgets the transaction.

12.6.3 State Machines

Coordinator states:

INIT: Transaction started, protocol not yet begun.

VOTING: PREPARE sent, waiting for votes.

DECIDED-COMMIT: Decision is COMMIT, log written, waiting for ACKs.

DECIDED-ABORT: Decision is ABORT, log written, waiting for ACKs.

DONE: All ACKs received, transaction forgotten.

Participant states:

INIT: Transaction started, processing.

PREPARED: Voted YES, log written, waiting for decision.

COMMITTED: Decision is COMMIT, log written, locks released.

ABORTED: Decision is ABORT (or local abort), log written, locks released.

12.6.4 Log Protocol

The log protocol is critical for crash recovery. Each node writes records that allow it to reconstruct its state after a crash.

Coordinator log records:

begin-coordinator (tid): Marks the start of the coordinator's role.

prepare (tid): Marks entry to VOTING state. (Optional; some implementations skip this.)

decision (tid, COMMIT | ABORT): The global decision. This record must be forced before the decision is sent to participants.

end (tid): All ACKs received; the coordinator can forget the transaction.

Participant log records:

begin-participant (tid): Marks the start of the participant's role.

prepared (tid): The participant voted YES. This record must be forced before the vote is sent. It contains the undo/redo information needed to complete or roll back the transaction after a crash.

commit (tid) or abort (tid): The global decision received from the coordinator. Forced before releasing locks (for commit) or before acknowledging.

12.6.5 Why the Log Protocol Is Correct

The prepared record is the linchpin. When a participant votes YES, it writes a prepared record (containing redo and undo information) and forces it to stable storage. This guarantees:

Durability: If the participant crashes after voting YES, upon recovery it finds the prepared record and knows it must complete the transaction (either commit or abort, depending on the coordinator's decision). It cannot forget the transaction.

Undoability: The prepared record contains enough information to roll back the transaction if the decision is ABORT.

Redoability: The prepared record contains enough information to redo the transaction if the decision is COMMIT and the participant crashes before writing its local changes to the database.

The decision record at the coordinator is similarly critical. The coordinator forces the decision to its log before sending it to participants. This guarantees that if the coordinator crashes after sending COMMIT to some participants, upon recovery it finds the decision record and can retransmit COMMIT to the remaining participants. Without the forced decision record, the coordinator might recover with no memory of the transaction, leaving participants in PREPARED state indefinitely (the "in-doubt transaction" problem).

12.6.6 Failure Analysis

We consider each failure point and show that 2PC maintains agreement.

Case 1: Participant crashes before voting YES.

The participant's state is volatile (no prepared record). Upon recovery, it has no memory of the transaction. The coordinator will time out waiting for the vote and decide ABORT. The participant, upon recovery, knows nothing and needs no recovery. Agreement holds: the transaction is aborted everywhere.

Case 2: Participant crashes after voting YES but before receiving the decision.

The participant has written a prepared record. Upon recovery, it finds the prepared record and enters PREPARED state. It must wait for the coordinator's decision. It sends a STATUS-QUERY (or simply waits for retransmission of the decision). The coordinator, if alive, retransmits the decision. If the coordinator has crashed, the participant remains blocked (see Case 4).

Case 3: Coordinator crashes before writing the decision record.

The coordinator has not decided. Upon recovery, it finds no decision record and decides ABORT (unilaterally, since it can always abort before deciding COMMIT). It sends ABORT to all participants. Agreement holds.

Case 4: Coordinator crashes after writing the decision record but before sending the decision to all participants.

The coordinator has decided (say, COMMIT) and has forced the decision record. Upon recovery, it finds the decision record and retransmits the decision to all participants. Participants that already received it are unaffected. Participants that have not received it will eventually receive it (from the recovering coordinator). Agreement holds.

However, there is a window: if the coordinator crashes after deciding COMMIT but before sending it to participant P, then P is blocked in PREPARED state until the coordinator recovers. P cannot unilaterally abort (it voted YES and cannot revoke its vote) and cannot unilaterally commit (it has not received the decision). P must wait.

This is the blocking problem. If the coordinator's crash is permanent (or long-lived), the participant's locks are held indefinitely, blocking other transactions. This is 2PC's fundamental weakness.

Case 5: Network partition between coordinator and participant.

If participant P is partitioned from the coordinator after P votes YES, P is blocked. When the partition heals, P can query the coordinator and receive the decision. If the partition is permanent, P is blocked indefinitely. This is equivalent to Case 4.

Case 6: Coordinator crashes after receiving all votes but before writing the decision record.

Same as Case 3: the coordinator recovers and aborts. Participants that voted YES are blocked until the recovering coordinator sends ABORT.

12.6.7 The Blocking Problem in Detail

The blocking problem arises because a participant in PREPARED state has delegated its decision to the coordinator. It cannot decide unilaterally because:

Unilateral abort is unsafe: If the coordinator has decided COMMIT and has sent COMMIT to other participants, then P's unilateral abort violates agreement. (P cannot know whether the coordinator decided.)

Unilateral commit is unsafe: If any other participant voted NO, the global decision is ABORT, and P's unilateral commit violates agreement.

The participant's dilemma is exactly the Two Generals problem: it cannot distinguish "coordinator decided COMMIT but the message was lost" from "coordinator decided ABORT but the message was lost" from "coordinator crashed before deciding." Without additional information, it must wait.

Termination protocol: In practice, systems implement a termination protocol to unblock participants when the coordinator is down. The simplest approach: when the coordinator recovers, it retransmits the decision. But if the coordinator's log is lost (e.g., the log disk is destroyed), the decision is unrecoverable, and participants are blocked forever. More sophisticated termination protocols (e.g., cooperative termination protocols) allow participants to query each other and decide based on collective knowledge, but these require additional protocol phases and do not eliminate blocking in all cases.

12.6.8 Three-Phase Commit (3PC)

Three-phase commit (Skeen, 1981) was proposed to eliminate 2PC's blocking problem. It adds a pre-commit phase between voting and commit, creating a state where all participants know that the transaction is "close to commit" and can safely commit unilaterally if the coordinator fails.

12.6.9 Protocol Description

Phase 1 (Voting): Same as 2PC. Participants vote YES/NO.

Phase 2 (Pre-commit): If all votes are YES, the coordinator sends PRE-COMMIT to all participants. Each participant, upon receiving PRE-COMMIT, writes a "pre-commit" record to its log and acknowledges. The participant is now in PRE-COMMITTED state.

Phase 3 (Commit): After receiving acknowledgments from all participants, the coordinator sends COMMIT (or DO-COMMIT) to all participants. Each participant, upon receiving COMMIT, writes a "commit" record, releases locks, and acknowledges.

12.6.10 Why 3PC Avoids Blocking

The key insight: In 3PC, no participant enters COMMITTED state until all participants have entered PRE-COMMITTED state. This means:

If a participant is in PRE-COMMITTED state, it knows that all participants voted YES and are prepared to commit. It can safely commit unilaterally (if the coordinator fails), because no participant can have voted NO (all voted YES in Phase 1) and no participant can have aborted.

If a participant is in PREPARED state (voted YES but has not received PRE-COMMIT), it can safely abort unilaterally (if the coordinator fails), because the coordinator cannot have decided COMMIT (it would have sent PRE-COMMIT first).

Thus, a participant's state determines its safe unilateral decision:

PREPARED → abort is safe.

PRE-COMMITTED → commit is safe.

ABORTED → abort is safe (trivially).

COMMITTED → commit is safe (trivially).

If the coordinator crashes, participants can run a termination protocol: they query each other's states and decide collectively. If any participant is in PRE-COMMITTED state, they all commit. If all are in PREPARED state, they all abort. No participant is ever blocked.

12.6.11 Why 3PC Is Impractical

3PC's correctness depends on the assumption that messages are delivered within a bounded time (or that timeouts fire "at the right time"). Specifically:

A participant in PREPARED state must know that the coordinator has not sent PRE-COMMIT. It uses a timeout to infer this. If the timeout fires prematurely (e.g., due to network delay), the participant aborts—potentially while the coordinator has decided COMMIT and other participants have committed. Agreement is violated.

A participant in PRE-COMMITTED state must know that all participants have received PRE-COMMIT. It uses a timeout to infer this. If the timeout fires prematurely, the participant commits—potentially while some participant has not yet received PRE-COMMIT and will abort. Agreement is violated.

In an asynchronous network (where messages can be delayed arbitrarily), 3PC cannot distinguish "slow message" from "crashed coordinator." This is exactly the FLP result: 3PC is a deterministic, terminating protocol, so it must give up asynchrony. It gives up asynchrony by assuming bounded message delay, and this assumption is what makes it correct.

In practice, networks are not perfectly synchronous, and 3PC's assumption is violated often enough that 3PC is rarely used. Instead, systems either accept 2PC's blocking (and implement recovery procedures) or use consensus-based commit (which is correct under partial synchrony and non-blocking).

12.6.12 Code: Two-Phase Commit in C

We now implement 2PC. The implementation uses:

A simple message layer with retransmission (to model an eventually-reliable network).

A log layer with forced writes (to model stable storage).

State machines for coordinator and participant.

Timeouts for liveness (to trigger abort on coordinator timeout and retransmission on participant timeout).

The code is single-threaded per node, using an event loop (select or epoll) to handle multiple connections. For clarity, we model each node as a separate process and use TCP sockets for communication.

/* In-memory log (for demonstration; real systems use a file or disk) */
#define LOG_MAX 1024

typedef struct {
    dt_logrec_t recs[LOG_MAX];
    int count;
} dt_log_t;

static dt_log_t g_log;

/* Append a record to the log and force it to stable storage. */
int log_append_force(ltype_t type, uint64_t tid, uint32_t data) {
    if (g_log.count >= LOG_MAX) {
        fprintf(stderr, "log full\n");
        return -1;
    }
    dt_logrec_t *r = &g_log.recs[g_log.count++];
    r->type = type;
    r->tid = tid;
    r->data = data;

    /* In a real system, this would be a write() + fsync() to a log file.
     * Here we simulate the cost with a small delay. */
    usleep(100);  /* 100 microseconds */
    return 0;
}

/* Scan the log for a record of a given type for a given tid. */
/* Returns 1 if found, 0 if not. */
int log_find(ltype_t type, uint64_t tid, uint32_t *data_out) {
    for (int i = 0; i < g_log.count; i++) {
        if (g_log.recs[i].type == type && g_log.recs[i].tid == tid) {
            if (data_out) *data_out = g_log.recs[i].data;
            return 1;
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

/* Print the log (for debugging). */
void log_dump(void) {
    printf("LOG DUMP (%d records):\n", g_log.count);
    for (int i = 0; i < g_log.count; i++) {
        dt_logrec_t *r = &g_log.recs[i];

#include "dt_common.h"

/* Simple TCP-based message layer. Each node listens on a port. */
/* Node ID i listens on port 9000 + i. */

#define BASE_PORT 9000

int net_listen(int node_id) {
    int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if (fd < 0) { perror("socket"); return -1; }

    int opt = 1;
    setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &opt, sizeof(opt));

    struct sockaddr_in addr;
    memset(&addr, 0, sizeof(addr));
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_addr.s_addr = INADDR_ANY;
    addr.sin_port = htons(BASE_PORT + node_id);

    if (bind(fd, (struct sockaddr*)&addr, sizeof(addr)) < 0) {
        perror("bind"); close(fd); return -1;
    }
    if (listen(fd, MAX_NODES) < 0) {
        perror("listen"); close(fd); return -1;
    }
    return fd;
}

int net_connect(int from_id, int to_id) {
    int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if (fd < 0) { perror("socket"); return -1; }

    struct sockaddr_in addr;
    memset(&addr, 0, sizeof(addr));
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_addr.s_addr = inet_addr("127.0.0.1");
    addr.sin_port = htons(BASE_PORT + to_id);

    if (connect(fd, (struct sockaddr*)&addr, sizeof(addr)) < 0) {
        perror("connect"); close(fd); return -1;
    }
    return fd;
}

/* Send a message. Returns 0 on success, -1 on failure. */
/* In a real system, this would be non-blocking with an output buffer. */
int net_send(int fd, dt_msg_t *msg) {
    ssize_t n = send(fd, msg, sizeof(*msg), 0);
    if (n != sizeof(*msg)) return -1;
    return 0;
}

/* Receive a message. Returns 1 on success, 0 if no message available, -1 on error. */
int net_recv(int fd, dt_msg_t *msg) {
    ssize_t n = recv(fd, msg, sizeof(*msg), MSG_DONTWAIT);
    if (n == sizeof(*msg)) return 1;
    if (n < 0 && (errno == EAGAIN || errno == EWOULDBLOCK)) return 0;
    return -1;
}

    g_txn.tid = tid;
    g_txn.state = CS_INIT;
    g_txn.n_participants = n_participants;

    g_txn.vote_deadline = now_ms() + VOTE_TIMEOUT_MS;
